title: Scoped Locking

validation.research: Five primary references: Douglas C. Schmidt’s original eight-page Scoped Locking idiom; the POSA Volume 2 author catalog; official Python threading and with-statement language documentation; Microsoft C++ scoped_lock documentation. Synchronized Block and Guard are historical aliases, with Guard distinguished from condition predicates and authorization checks. RAII is identified as a broader resource-management idiom rather than an exact alias. Scope-bound acquisition/release, named C++ guard lifetime, successful-entry precondition, supported return/exception cleanup and release-versus-rollback are explicit. C++17 scoped_lock’s multi-mutex acquisition algorithm is kept distinct from the general pattern and Python nested with blocks. Original paper and official documentation support the mechanism; the inventory scenario, immutable publication, code and diagrams are original teaching material.

runnable_example.verification: Exact four-line demo output; invalid initial/request counts reject Boolean and malformed values before acquisition; zero stock, exact exhaustion and insufficient-stock boundaries preserve coherent state; one persistent real Lock per object and no object-created worker; real lock instrumentation verifies exactly paired entry/exit on return, snapshot, rejection and propagated ordinary/BaseException failures; failed-entry injection performs no body or unmatched release; a gated acquisition blocks a competing caller before check/publication; a gated post-release exit permits another caller to snapshot before the original return is delivered; faults before publication leave old state while faults after publication preserve changed coherent state, proving release is not rollback; four actual reservers make 240 attempts with exactly 120 unique successful states and 120 rejections while an additional reader observes 200 snapshots, with invariant checks at every release and no overlapping protected ownership; locks are independent between instances, a nonblocking recursive acquisition probe fails, every lock is available afterward, all caller threads join and thread inventory returns to baseline. Instrumentation wraps actual Lock and attribute-access seams without replacing article reservation/snapshot methods. No fairness, automatic rollback, general deadlock avoidance, acquisition deadline, async-task or cross-process guarantee is inferred.

example_limits: Original Python 3.11+ synchronous Inventory with one persistent plain nonreentrant Lock per instance. Nonnegative integer initial stock and positive integer reservation requests reject Boolean values. A with scope protects both the available-count check and immutable available/reserved tuple publication, preserving nonnegative counts and initial total on expected paths. Success returns inside the block, insufficient stock raises before publication, and snapshot reads use the same lock. Cleanup releases before result delivery or exception observation; snapshot values are immutable point-in-time observations, not live state. The demo owns and joins one separate caller thread outside any lock scope. Tests verify exact output, validation boundaries, zero/exhausted stock, real contention, failed-entry behavior without unmatched release, return delivery after release, ordinary/BaseException cleanup, before/after-publication faults showing that release is not rollback, and 240 concurrent reservation attempts yielding 120 unique successes and 120 rejections alongside 200 extra reader snapshots, with invariant checks at every release. Independent object locks, nonrecursive acquisition probe, balanced acquisitions/releases, available locks after every case and all caller-thread joins are verified. Instrumented seams wrap real locks and attribute access without replacing reservation/snapshot methods. Callers must follow public locking protocol and keep the lock alive. No acquisition deadline, fairness, general lock-order/deadlock freedom, rollback, async-task lock behavior, cross-process atomicity or process-failure recovery is claimed. A stuck body can retain the lock; manually releasing the same acquisition or bypassing the protocol is unsupported.
